props.title: White Light/Black Rain: The Destruction of Hiroshima and Nagasaki
props.initialSlug: The unforgettable story of two cities.

sections.content: White Light/Black Rain (2007) stands as one of the most powerful nuclear holocaust documentaries ever made. Director Steven Okazaki interviews 14 survivors (hibakusha) of the atomic bombings, creating an unflinching record of firsthand accounts. The film's power comes from its direct approach, letting survivors tell their stories while incorporating rare archival footage, including previously classified material. This documentary pairs naturally with The Day After (1983), which shocked 100 million American viewers with its depiction of nuclear war's aftermath, and Threads (1984), the BBC's brutally realistic portrayal of nuclear devastation.

sections.content: The impact of nuclear weapons on Japanese cinema cannot be overstated. Godzilla (1954) emerged as a direct metaphor for atomic devastation, with its scenes of mass destruction echoing recent memories of Hiroshima and Nagasaki. This launched an entire kaiju genre dealing with atomic anxiety. Documentary approaches evolved from propaganda films like The Effects of the Atomic Bomb on Hiroshima and Nagasaki (1946) to more critical works like Hiroshima Mon Amour (1959), which explored the psychological aftermath through an intimate lens.

Modern nuclear documentaries like Command and Control (2016) and Countdown to Zero (2010) build on White Light/Black Rain's foundation by examining how close we've come to accidental nuclear disasters. These films connect the historical reality of Hiroshima and Nagasaki to ongoing nuclear threats, while works like The Man Who Saved the World (2014) highlight individuals who helped prevent nuclear catastrophe. sections.content: White Light/Black Rain's influence extends beyond its subject matter to documentary technique. Its approach of letting survivors speak directly to camera, minimizing narrator intervention, influenced later historical documentaries like The Act of Killing (2012) and The Look of Silence (2014). The film's use of restored archival footage and survivor artwork created a template for documenting historical trauma that later films like They Shall Not Grow Old (2018) would follow.
